questions.q: Per this lesson, what is a governance framework's purpose relative to the individual topics covered in Chapters 1 and 2?
options: It ties all those individually-covered pieces together into one coherent, referenceable whole, so the program doesn't rely on scattered memory or tribal knowledge
It replaces the need for ownership, stewardship, retention, and classification policies entirely
It is a purely technical document with no connection to data-governance topics
It only applies to orgs with fewer than 100 users
questions.explain: The framework is explicitly described as the single document (or set of documents) that assembles the separately-covered pieces into one coherent, referenceable whole.

questions.q: What are the four connected areas a Center of Excellence (CoE) model typically organizes a Salesforce governance framework's scope into, per this lesson?
options: Marketing, Sales, Finance, and Support
Encryption, backups, APIs, and licensing only
Org strategy, data governance, technical governance, and change management
Hiring, budgeting, vendor management, and office space
questions.explain: The CoE model frames governance across org strategy (vision/prioritization), data governance (Ch. 1-2 topics), technical governance (code/config standards), and change management (the deployment lifecycle).

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue a governance framework needs to address release/change strategy, not just data policy topics?
options: Release strategy is unrelated to data governance and shouldn't be mentioned in the same document
Data governance frameworks are legally required to never mention deployment processes
Release strategy only matters for orgs using Shield

A new field or change can go live without anyone checking whether it needs classification or fits an existing retention policy, unless a data-governance checkpoint is built into the existing release gate
questions.explain: Without a data-governance checkpoint inside the release gate, new risk (an unclassified field, a field that should feed a retention policy) can enter the org with nothing stopping it.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a statement like "the admin team reviews changes" is too vague to be useful?
options: Because it doesn't survive contact with a real dispute about who actually has final say -- a usable framework names a specific role for each approval point
Because admin teams are never allowed to review changes under any governance model
Because only a single named individual, never a team, can ever hold approval authority
Because the statement is grammatically incorrect
questions.explain: The lesson states vague accountability is functionally the same as no accountability -- it just takes longer to discover that during an actual crisis, which is why specific roles need to be named.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe a governance framework as a "living document" rather than a one-time deliverable?
options: Because Salesforce requires framework documents to be resubmitted annually to Salesforce support
Because living documents are a specific Salesforce file type
Because it degrades the same way an unreviewed classification label or unmonitored quality metric does, unless it has an owner and a scheduled review to keep it matching how the org actually operates
Because a framework document expires automatically after 180 days like Setup Audit Trail
questions.explain: The lesson draws a direct parallel to the recurring theme from Chapters 1-2: anything not reviewed on a schedule quietly stops matching reality, and a framework needs the same ongoing ownership.
